stops.name: Berlin, Schloss Tegel, birth of "the little apothecary"
stops.campa: In the family seat at Tegel, east of Berlin, a second son is born to the Prussian officer Alexander Georg von Humboldt and Marie-Elisabeth von Holwede on the fourteenth of September. He and his elder brother Wilhelm are raised among tutors, herbaria and the flat Brandenburg woods; the boy collects plants and insects so relentlessly that the household nicknames him der kleine Apotheker, the little apothecary. Berlin gives him rigor; Tegel gives him the taste for the wild that will carry him, one day, to two hemispheres and every latitude between them.

stops.name: Mainz, setting out with Georg Forster
stops.campa: At twenty, already restless in the university towns of Frankfurt and Göttingen, Humboldt attaches himself to Georg Forster, the naturalist who sailed round the world with Cook, and sets out with him from Mainz down the Rhine and on through Brabant, Holland, England and revolutionary Paris. It is his first true expedition, four months of rivers, ports and a continent in ferment, and Forster's example, the scientist as traveler and the traveler as writer, becomes the pattern of the life not yet chosen. He dedicates his first paper, on the basalts of the Rhine, to his companion.

stops.name: Freiberg, the Bergakademie, the mines of Saxony
stops.campa: At the Freiberg School of Mines Humboldt drives himself without mercy: mornings underground among the Saxon galleries, five or six hours of lecture in the afternoon, the surrounding country combed for plants by candle-light and moonlight after that. He masters mineralogy and geology under Werner in barely a year, leaves in 1792 without troubling to take a degree, and is at once appointed a Prussian inspector of mines, a post he uses, over the following years, to invent a safety lamp and a rescue apparatus for miners, and to keep training the eye that will one day read the strata of two continents.

stops.name: Berlin, the death of the mother, the fortune, the resignation
stops.campa: Marie-Elisabeth von Humboldt dies on the nineteenth of November; neither son attends the funeral, for the coldness between mother and sons has never thawed, and one of Alexander's correspondents writes bluntly that her death must be welcome to him. It is, in the plainest sense: brother and sister divide a considerable fortune, and Alexander is at last free of the civil service and of every obligation but his own curiosity. Within the year he resigns his post as mining inspector and begins, in earnest, to plan the journey no one yet knows will be to the Americas.

stops.name: Jena, four thousand experiments in galvanism
stops.campa: Freed and restless, Humboldt lodges at Jena and throws himself at the new mystery of the age: galvanism, the electricity of living tissue. Over months he runs some four thousand experiments on frogs, on muscle and nerve, on his own arms and back, applying zinc and silver to broken skin until he blisters and bleeds, chasing Volta's and Galvani's quarrel toward an answer neither man had reached. He publishes the results as Versuche über die gereizte Muskel- und Nervenfaser: proof, to himself at least, that the living body is a theatre of chemistry and force, not a machine apart from nature.

stops.name: Weimar, Goethe's blessing, the taste for science reawakened
stops.campa: From Jena Humboldt walks the short road to Weimar and renews an old acquaintance with Goethe, minister and poet, who is drawn at once to the young man's electric energy and his galvanic apparatus. They perform experiments together at Goethe's house; Goethe will write that this remarkable young man deserves credit for having again aroused his own taste for natural science, dormant since his Italian years. Schiller too receives him. The circle that will one day place Schelling in Jena's chair is already forming around Humboldt's frogs and batteries: the last German constellation he sees before he leaves for the Americas.
stops.quote: The young Baron von Humboldt... deserves great credit for having again aroused my taste for natural science, which had lain dormant.

stops.name: Madrid, the passport of a king
stops.campa: Two expeditions fail him first, Egypt closed by Napoleon's campaign, a Mediterranean crossing blocked by war, before Humboldt and the Prussian minister at Madrid, Baron von Forell, manage what no foreigner has managed in generations: an audience with the court of Carlos IV and a royal passport opening every Spanish American possession to a private traveler's instruments and curiosity. The French botanist Aimé Bonpland, met by chance in Paris, is already his companion. Humboldt calls the permission unheard-of liberality; within weeks the two men are on the road to Galicia and the sea.

stops.name: La Coruña, the Pizarro sails
stops.campa: On the fifth of June, at the Galician port of A Coruña, Humboldt and Bonpland carry aboard the corvette Pizarro a small observatory of instruments: sextants, barometers, a dipping needle, a cyanometer of Humboldt's own invention to measure the blue of the sky. War and an English blockade delay the sailing three weeks more. When the ship finally clears the harbor it is bound, nominally, for Havana; fever aboard and a young Asturian dead of it will change that plan before the month is out, and send them instead toward a coast neither man has any commission to visit.

stops.name: Tenerife, the summit of the Teide
stops.campa: A stop meant only for water becomes six days of wonder. Humboldt and Bonpland climb through vineyards and pine forest and pumice to the crater of the Teide on 21 June, sleep near the rim, and descend at dawn with the volcano rising clear above a sea of cloud, the first sunbeams touching its summit before they touch the men below. Humboldt will call the view from Tenerife's western coast the loveliest he has known in either hemisphere. Geobotany, the mapping of plant life by altitude and climate, the discipline that will govern his whole science, is born on this single mountainside.
stops.quote: I have never beheld a prospect more varied, more attractive, more harmonious in the distribution of the masses of verdure and of rocks, than the western coast of Teneriffe.
stops.quote_source: Personal Narrative of Travels to the Equinoctial Regions of the New Continent, vol. 1 (1814)

stops.name: CUMANÁ, landfall on the Spanish Main
stops.campa: Forty-one days from Tenerife, sickness aboard turns the Pizarro from its course, and on 16 July Humboldt and Bonpland step ashore not at Havana but at Cumaná, on the pearl coast of Nueva Andalucía, the oldest Spanish town on the continent and a place that already holds, four years old and playing in its streets, a boy named Antonio José de Sucre, who will die a Marshal of Ayacucho. Humboldt is dazzled by the light, the coconut palms, the ease of a colonial world he has read of only in books; he calls it the true beginning of the New World for him.
stops.quote: The splendour of the day, the vivid colouring of the vegetable world, the forms of the plants, the varied plumage of the birds, everything was stamped with the grand character of nature in the equinoctial regions.
stops.quote_source: Personal Narrative of Travels to the Equinoctial Regions of the New Continent, vol. 1 (1814)

stops.name: Caracas, arrival at the shadow of the Silla
stops.campa: After four months among the missions and llanos east of Cumaná, Humboldt and Bonpland ride into Caracas on 21 November, guests of the Aristeguieta and Ustáriz families, in a city that still counts its notable sons in single figures. A sixteen-year-old orphan named Simón Bolívar has sailed for Spain only months before. Humboldt lodges in the cool of the valley beneath the great mountain wall the Caraqueños call la Silla, the saddle, and asks its height. No one can tell him: no one has climbed it. He resolves, within days of arriving, to be the first.

stops.name: Silla de Caracas, the first ascent
stops.campa: No creole gentleman or curious amateur will risk the climb, so Humboldt hires sixteen enslaved men from the Blandín estate to cut a path up the ravines between Chacaíto and Quintero. On 2 January, barometer in hand, he and Bonpland reach the Pico Oriental of the Silla and become the first men of record to stand on it. His mercury barometer gives 2,660 meters, twenty meters from the height accepted today. From the summit the whole Caribbean coast and the green trough of the valley lie mapped beneath him for the first time in human knowledge.
